1) Kaposi sarcoma (patch-stage) — Most likely. Rationale: chronic, slowly expanding violaceous patches/plaques in a young adult; histology showing irregular, anastomosing/thin‑walled vascular channels dissecting through dermal collagen with plump endothelial cells and CD34 positivity is classic for early Kaposi. Key next steps (confirmatory): immunohistochemistry for HHV‑8 (LANA‑1) on the biopsy and HIV testing (4th‑generation antigen/antibody) with CD4 count/viral load if positive.

2) Cutaneous angiosarcoma (low‑grade) — Less likely but important to consider. Rationale: angiosarcoma can show irregular, dissecting vascular channels; would usually show cytologic atypia/mitoses (not seen here), but sampling error can miss higher‑grade areas. Recommendation: expert dermatopathology review, additional deeper sections and proliferation index (Ki‑67), and endothelial markers (CD31, ERG) if concern persists.

3) Pseudo‑Kaposi / Acroangiodermatitis — Possible alternative. Rationale: benign reactive vascular proliferation can mimic Kaposi clinically and histologically; typically associated with venous stasis or arteriovenous shunting. Evaluate for local venous hypertension (venous/arterial duplex ultrasound of the left upper limb).

4) Epithelioid hemangioma (including hobnail/targetoid hemosiderotic hemangioma variants) — Less likely. Rationale: benign vascular tumors can produce violaceous plaques and show plump endothelial cells; histology usually has characteristic lobular architecture and often eosinophils. Correlate with additional endothelial markers (CD31), review for inflammatory infiltrate/eosinophils.

5) Tufted angioma / kaposiform hemangioendothelioma — Unlikely but worth listing. Rationale: vascular lobules/tufts can dissect dermis; usually seen in children/young infants but occasionally present later. Histologic pattern differs (cannonball tufts) — review biopsy for that pattern.

Recommended immediate actions (clinical): obtain HHV‑8 LANA‑1 stain on the submitted biopsy, perform HIV 4th‑generation test, request an expert dermatopathology read if HHV‑8 negative or if angiosarcoma remains a concern, and perform a full skin exam and local vascular Doppler of the left upper limb. If HHV‑8 positive or HIV positive, refer to dermatology/oncology for staging and treatment discussion.
